key_insight: Pretrained protein language models (pLMs) can unintentionally leak dataset-specific information into downstream protein–protein interaction (PPI) models, producing artificially inflated performance metrics. Szymborski & Emad demonstrate and quantify this leakage risk in common PPI evaluation setups.
problem_solved: Identifies and diagnoses a hidden source of data leakage when using pLM-derived features for PPI inference, which can mislead model evaluation and mask lack of true generalization.
method: Systematic analysis showing that embeddings from pretrained pLMs carry dataset- or family-specific signals that can be exploited by PPI classifiers.
Controlled experiments and ablations comparing standard evaluations to leakage-aware partitions and baseline controls to quantify the magnitude of performance inflation.

Recommendations for evaluation best practices and mitigation strategies (e.g., stricter train/test partitioning, randomized baselines, and leakage checks) to obtain reliable PPI performance estimates.
impact: Raises an important caution for AI/ML practitioners using pretrained pLMs in biological tasks: reported gains may be partially due to leakage, so rigorous evaluation protocols and explicit leakage controls are essential to ensure real biological generalization.
visual_elements: Flow diagram: pretrained pLM → embeddings → downstream PPI model, with an annotated ‘leakage’ pathway highlighted
Bar chart comparing reported (leaked) vs corrected (leakage-mitigated) model performance
Embedding similarity heatmap or t-SNE/UMAP showing clusters that reveal dataset-specific signals in pLM embeddings
Checklist/infographic panel of recommended evaluation controls (split rules, baselines, ablations)
paper_title: A flaw in using pretrained protein language models in protein–protein interaction inference models
